exam2.question: A transcranial Doppler exam after head trauma shows a left MCA mean velocity of 140 cm/s. The left extracranial internal carotid artery mean velocity is 70 cm/s, and velocities are similarly elevated on the right. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Hyperemia, because the Lindegaard ratio is 2.0
Severe MCA vasospasm, because the MCA mean velocity exceeds 120 cm/s
Distal MCA occlusion, because the ratio is below 3
Moderate vasospasm, because the Lindegaard ratio is 4.0

exam2.explanation: The Lindegaard ratio is 140 / 70 = 2.0; a ratio below 3 with elevated MCA velocity indicates that velocities are high in both the intracranial and extracranial vessels, which reflects increased global flow (hyperemia) rather than focal narrowing. An MCA mean velocity above 120 cm/s alone cannot distinguish vasospasm from hyperemia, which is the purpose of the ratio.
exam2.hint: Ask whether the high velocity is confined to the intracranial vessel or present upstream as well.

exam2.question: During transcranial Doppler emboli monitoring of the MCA during carotid endarterectomy, which feature is characteristic of a microembolic signal (high-intensity transient signal)?

options.text: A continuous, symmetric signal above and below the baseline throughout the cardiac cycle
A gradual rise in mean velocity lasting several minutes
A low-intensity signal that appears only at end diastole in every beat
A brief, unidirectional, high-intensity signal within the spectrum with a chirp or click sound

exam2.explanation: Microembolic signals are short (usually under 300 ms), unidirectional, at least about 3 dB more intense than the background blood flow signal, occur randomly in the cardiac cycle and produce a characteristic chirp or click. Artifacts from movement or probe tapping are typically bidirectional and symmetric about the baseline, which helps distinguish them from true emboli.
exam2.hint: An embolus is a strong reflector traveling with the blood for only a moment.

exam2.question: A patient has a severe stenosis of the proximal right internal carotid artery. A transorbital Doppler exam on the right shows ophthalmic artery flow directed away from the transducer, while the left ophthalmic artery flows toward the transducer. What does the right-sided finding indicate?

options.text: Occlusion of the right ophthalmic artery
Collateral flow from the external carotid artery through orbital branches into the intracranial ICA
Normal flow direction in the right ophthalmic artery
Cross-filling from the left ICA through the anterior communicating artery

exam2.explanation: Normally the ophthalmic artery flows from the ICA toward the orbit, toward the transducer. When the ICA pressure drops distal to a severe stenosis, ECA branches (facial, superficial temporal, maxillary) feed the orbit and reverse ophthalmic flow back into the siphon, so flow moves away from the probe. Anterior communicating artery cross-filling would show up as reversed flow in the ipsilateral A1 segment, not in the ophthalmic artery.
exam2.hint: Consider which pressure is now higher: the orbit's external carotid supply or the ICA beyond the lesion.

exam2.question: Reversed flow is found in the left ophthalmic artery of a patient with suspected left ICA occlusion. Which maneuver best confirms that the reversed flow is supplied by the external carotid artery?

options.text: Brief compression of the ipsilateral superficial temporal or facial artery while monitoring the ophthalmic signal
Compression of the ipsilateral common carotid artery for 30 seconds
Having the patient perform a Valsalva maneuver
Inflating a blood pressure cuff on the left arm

exam2.explanation: If the reversed ophthalmic flow is fed by ECA branches, briefly compressing the superficial temporal or facial artery will reduce, abolish or reverse the ophthalmic signal, confirming the ECA source. Common carotid compression is not used as a routine maneuver because it can dislodge plaque and cause a stroke, and it would not isolate the ECA branches.
exam2.hint: Interrupt one of the small branches that could be feeding the orbit and watch whether the signal changes.

exam2.question: A patient has an occluded right internal carotid artery. On transcranial Doppler through the right temporal window, which finding best indicates that the right hemisphere is receiving collateral flow from the left ICA through the anterior communicating artery?

options.text: Normal flow away from the transducer in the right A1 segment
Reversed flow in the right ophthalmic artery
Flow toward the transducer in the right A1 segment
Increased pulsatility in the right posterior cerebral artery

exam2.explanation: Normally the A1 segment flows away from the ipsilateral temporal probe; when blood crosses from the left through the anterior communicating artery, it travels backward down the right A1 toward the right terminal ICA, so the flow is directed toward the transducer. The left A1 typically shows elevated velocity because it carries the extra flow. Reversed ophthalmic flow indicates ECA collateral, a different pathway.
exam2.hint: Picture the direction blood must travel in the A1 segment to reach the right MCA from the opposite side.

exam2.question: Which statement about the anatomy of the circle of Willis is most accurate?

options.text: It is complete and symmetric in nearly all adults
A complete, well-formed circle is present in fewer than half of people
It connects only the two internal carotid arteries, not the vertebrobasilar system
It lies within the cavernous sinus on each side of the sella

exam2.explanation: Anatomic variants such as a hypoplastic or absent communicating artery or A1 segment, or a fetal-origin posterior cerebral artery, are common, and a complete, symmetric circle is found in less than half of the population. This variability explains why collateral capacity after carotid occlusion differs greatly between patients. The circle links the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems through the posterior communicating arteries and lies in the subarachnoid space at the base of the brain.
exam2.hint: Variations in this structure explain why two patients with the same carotid occlusion can have very different outcomes.

exam2.question: From which artery does the ophthalmic artery normally arise?

options.text: Maxillary branch of the external carotid artery
Proximal middle cerebral artery
A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery
Internal carotid artery, as its first major intracranial branch

exam2.explanation: The ophthalmic artery normally arises from the internal carotid artery as it exits the cavernous sinus, making it the first major intracranial branch of the ICA. Its connections with ECA branches around the orbit are what allow it to serve as an important ECA-to-ICA collateral pathway; it does not normally arise from the ECA itself.
exam2.hint: This vessel is the link that lets orbital branches of the external system communicate with the carotid siphon.

exam2.question: A 66-year-old smoker has coolness and fatigue of the left hand with use. Upper extremity segmental pressures are: right upper arm 152 mmHg, right forearm 148 mmHg, left upper arm 150 mmHg and left forearm 112 mmHg. Where is the most likely site of disease?

options.text: Left subclavian artery
Right subclavian or innominate artery
No significant disease; this is normal variation
Left distal brachial artery or proximal forearm arteries

exam2.explanation: The upper arm pressures are equal on both sides, which argues against inflow disease in the subclavian, innominate or axillary arteries. A pressure drop of more than about 10 to 15 mmHg between adjacent cuff levels on the same arm suggests disease between them; here the left arm drops 38 mmHg from the upper arm to the forearm, localizing the lesion to the distal brachial artery or the proximal radial and ulnar arteries. The right arm shows a normal small gradient.
exam2.hint: Compare adjacent levels on the same arm as well as the two arms at the same level.

exam2.question: Which spectral Doppler waveform is expected in the brachial artery distal to a hemodynamically significant proximal subclavian artery stenosis?

options.text: Monophasic, dampened waveform with a delayed systolic upstroke
Sharp triphasic waveform with high peak systolic velocity
High-resistance waveform with prominent diastolic flow reversal
Aliased waveform with marked spectral broadening

exam2.explanation: Distal to a significant stenosis, the pressure and flow are reduced and peripheral vessels dilate, producing a monophasic, low-amplitude waveform with a slow upstroke (tardus parvus). A normal resting upper extremity artery is triphasic or multiphasic with a sharp upstroke; high velocities with aliasing and broadening are found at or just beyond the stenosis, not far downstream.
exam2.hint: Think about what happens to waveform shape well downstream of a pressure-reducing lesion.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old swimmer has arm pain and finger pallor when working overhead. What is the most appropriate noninvasive technique to evaluate for arterial thoracic outlet compression?

options.text: Cold water immersion of the hand with digit temperature recovery
Segmental arm pressures with the arm at rest only
Arterial Doppler or digit PPG waveforms recorded in neutral and then in provocative positions such as arm abduction and elevation with head rotation
Compression ultrasound of the subclavian and axillary veins

exam2.explanation: Arterial thoracic outlet compression is often positional, so waveforms are recorded at rest and then during provocative maneuvers that narrow the costoclavicular or interscalene spaces; a marked dampening or loss of signal that reproduces symptoms supports the diagnosis. Resting studies alone are frequently normal, and cold immersion evaluates vasospasm rather than mechanical compression. Because some normal people also show positional dampening, results must be correlated with symptoms.
exam2.hint: The compression in this condition appears only when the arm is placed in certain positions.

exam2.question: A 28-year-old woman has sudden pain and a cool, pale index finger. Imaging shows a cervical rib on the same side. Duplex shows a focal fusiform dilation of the subclavian artery just distal to the rib with mural thrombus. What is the most likely explanation of her finger symptoms?

options.text: Primary Raynaud phenomenon triggered by cold exposure
Embolization from a post-stenotic subclavian aneurysm caused by arterial thoracic outlet compression
Subclavian steal from a proximal subclavian occlusion
Venous thoracic outlet syndrome with subclavian vein thrombosis

exam2.explanation: Repeated compression of the subclavian artery by a cervical rib causes post-stenotic dilation or aneurysm formation, and thrombus within the aneurysm can embolize to the hand and fingers. Primary Raynaud phenomenon is bilateral, episodic and does not involve a structural arterial lesion, and venous thrombosis would cause arm swelling rather than digital ischemia.
exam2.hint: Connect the bony abnormality, the dilated arterial segment and the sudden distal ischemia.

exam2.question: During cold immersion testing, digit temperatures are recorded before immersion and then every few minutes after the hands are removed from ice water. In a patient with episodic finger color changes, it takes 30 minutes for digit temperatures to return to the pre-immersion baseline. How is this result best interpreted?

options.text: Abnormal; delayed recovery consistent with cold-induced vasospasm such as Raynaud phenomenon
Normal; recovery normally takes 30 to 45 minutes
Abnormal; diagnostic of a fixed radial artery occlusion
Nondiagnostic; cold immersion cannot assess digital vasospasm

exam2.explanation: In normal subjects, digit temperature typically returns to baseline within about 10 minutes after cold immersion; a markedly prolonged recovery supports cold-induced vasospasm. The test does not localize or diagnose a fixed proximal arterial occlusion, which is better assessed with pressures, waveforms or duplex imaging.
exam2.hint: Think about how quickly digit temperature should return to baseline in a healthy hand after a cold challenge.

exam2.question: Before a radial artery is harvested for coronary bypass, a PPG sensor is placed on the thumb and the radial artery is compressed at the wrist. The thumb waveform becomes flat and stays flat until compression is released. What does this finding indicate?

options.text: Normal result; flattening is expected with radial compression
An ulnar artery stenosis at the wrist that does not affect the hand
Technical error caused by sensor placement on the thumb
Incomplete palmar arch with the thumb dependent on radial flow, making harvest risky

exam2.explanation: In this modified Allen test, a complete palmar arch allows the ulnar artery to maintain digit perfusion when the radial artery is compressed, so the waveform is preserved or only mildly reduced. Loss of the thumb waveform shows that the ulnar supply does not adequately reach the radial side of the hand, so removing the radial artery could cause hand ischemia.
exam2.hint: Ask what supplies the thumb once the radial artery is taken out of the circuit.

exam2.question: A 45-year-old mechanic who routinely strikes tools with the heel of his hand has pain and color changes in his ring and little fingers of the dominant hand. Which finding on duplex is most likely?

options.text: Radial artery dissection at the anatomic snuffbox
Ulnar artery aneurysm or thrombosis near the hook of the hamate
Brachial artery entrapment at the elbow
Subclavian artery occlusion with reversed vertebral flow

exam2.explanation: Hypothenar hammer syndrome results from repetitive trauma to the ulnar artery where it passes over the hook of the hamate, causing aneurysm or thrombosis and emboli to the ulnar-sided fingers. A subclavian occlusion would usually cause arm claudication and would not selectively affect the fourth and fifth fingers of a manual worker's dominant hand.
exam2.hint: Think about which artery lies exposed over a bony prominence of the hypothenar eminence.

exam2.question: Duplex in a 74-year-old man shows a true aneurysm of the common femoral artery measuring 2.6 cm. What additional evaluation is most appropriate?

options.text: Venous reflux study of the ipsilateral leg
Carotid duplex to exclude dissection
Duplex of the abdominal aorta and both popliteal arteries
No further imaging, since femoral aneurysms occur in isolation

exam2.explanation: True femoral artery aneurysms are frequently associated with aneurysms elsewhere, especially of the abdominal aorta and the popliteal arteries, and are often bilateral. Screening those sites is therefore standard. Femoral aneurysms are rarely isolated, and a venous reflux study does not address the arterial disease.
exam2.hint: Degenerative aneurysmal disease tends to appear at more than one site in the same patient.

exam2.question: Which is the most common visceral artery aneurysm, and which group has a particularly high risk of rupture?

options.text: Hepatic artery aneurysm; elderly men
Superior mesenteric artery aneurysm; patients with cirrhosis
Splenic artery aneurysm; pregnant women
Renal artery aneurysm; young athletes

exam2.explanation: The splenic artery is the most common site of visceral artery aneurysm, and these aneurysms are more frequent in women. Rupture during pregnancy, especially in the third trimester, carries high maternal and fetal mortality, so repair is generally advised in women of childbearing age. Hepatic artery aneurysms are the second most common.
exam2.hint: This aneurysm often appears as a calcified ring in the left upper quadrant and is linked to hormonal and hemodynamic changes.

exam2.question: An iatrogenic arteriovenous fistula between the right common femoral artery and vein is confirmed after cardiac catheterization. Compared with the normal left common femoral artery, which spectral waveform is most expected in the right common femoral artery proximal to the fistula?

options.text: Low-resistance waveform with elevated velocity and continuous forward flow in diastole
Normal triphasic, high-resistance waveform unchanged from the left side
Sharp systolic peak with reversed flow throughout diastole
Dampened tardus-parvus waveform with low peak systolic velocity

exam2.explanation: The fistula is a low-resistance shunt directly into the vein, so the artery feeding it loses its normal triphasic, high-resistance pattern and shows increased velocity with continuous forward diastolic flow. The artery beyond the fistula may keep a more normal pattern or show reduced flow. A tardus-parvus waveform reflects a proximal stenosis, and diastolic flow reversal reflects high downstream resistance, the opposite of a shunt.
exam2.hint: Think about the resistance of the circuit the artery is now feeding.

exam2.question: Reynolds number predicts when laminar flow will become turbulent. Which change, with all other factors constant, increases the Reynolds number and the likelihood of turbulence?

options.text: Decreased flow velocity
Decreased blood viscosity, as in severe anemia
Decreased vessel diameter at the same velocity
Increased blood viscosity, as in polycythemia

exam2.explanation: Reynolds number equals density times velocity times diameter divided by viscosity, so lowering viscosity raises the Reynolds number; turbulence generally appears above about 2000. This is why anemic patients can have flow murmurs without stenosis. Decreasing velocity or diameter, or increasing viscosity, lowers the Reynolds number.
exam2.hint: Write out the Reynolds number formula and see which term sits in the denominator.

exam2.question: In steady laminar flow with a fully developed parabolic profile, how does the mean (spatial average) velocity compare with the peak velocity at the center of the vessel?

options.text: The mean velocity equals the peak velocity
The mean velocity is twice the peak velocity
The mean velocity is about 90 percent of the peak velocity
The mean velocity is half the peak velocity

exam2.explanation: In a parabolic profile, velocity is highest at the center and falls to near zero at the wall, and the spatial average works out to one half of the centerline velocity. The mean equals the peak only in an idealized plug profile, where all layers move at nearly the same speed.
exam2.hint: Picture the velocity layers ranging from zero at the wall to maximum in the center.

exam2.question: Plug flow is present in the proximal ascending aorta. Which spectral Doppler appearance best reflects this flow profile?

options.text: A thin spectral trace with a large, clear window beneath it
A filled-in spectrum with flow above and below the baseline
A broad spectrum with the window completely filled during systole
A low-amplitude waveform with a delayed upstroke

exam2.explanation: In plug flow nearly all red cells move at the same velocity across the lumen, so the spectrum shows a narrow band of frequencies with a clear spectral window. A filled-in or broadened spectrum indicates a wide range of velocities, as seen with disturbed or turbulent flow, or with a parabolic profile sampled by a large sample volume.
exam2.hint: Ask how wide the range of red cell velocities is when the whole column moves together.

exam2.question: As blood passes through an arterial stenosis, where do the greatest inertial energy losses occur?

options.text: At the entrance of the stenosis, where flow accelerates
Evenly along the entire length of the narrowed segment
At the exit of the stenosis, where the jet expands with flow separation and turbulence
In the normal artery several centimeters proximal to the stenosis

exam2.explanation: Inertial losses come from changes in velocity and direction and are proportional to the velocity squared. They are largest at the outlet, where the high-velocity jet abruptly decelerates and expands, producing flow separation, eddies and turbulence. Viscous losses, in contrast, are distributed along the length of the narrowed segment.
exam2.hint: Energy is wasted most where the orderly jet breaks up into eddies.

exam2.question: According to Poiseuille's law, if the length of a narrowed arterial segment increases from 1 cm to 4 cm while its radius and the blood viscosity remain unchanged, how does the resistance of that segment change?

options.text: It decreases to one quarter
It stays the same
It increases 16 times
It increases 4 times

exam2.explanation: Poiseuille's law gives resistance as 8 times viscosity times length divided by pi times the radius to the fourth power, so resistance is directly proportional to length. Quadrupling the length quadruples the resistance. A 16-fold change would occur if the radius were halved, because radius acts to the fourth power.
exam2.hint: Length appears in the numerator of the resistance formula without an exponent.

exam2.question: A patient has a 45 percent diameter iliac artery stenosis that causes no pressure drop at rest. During exercise, the leg vessels dilate and flow increases. How does this affect the lesion's hemodynamic significance?

options.text: The lesion becomes less significant because higher flow opens the stenosis
The lesion can become significant, because critical stenosis occurs at a smaller degree of narrowing when flow increases and distal resistance falls
Its significance is unchanged, because critical stenosis is a fixed 50 percent diameter reduction
The lesion becomes significant only if blood viscosity also increases

exam2.explanation: Critical stenosis is not a fixed value; it depends on flow rate and downstream resistance. When peripheral resistance drops and flow increases with exercise, the pressure gradient across a lesion rises, so a stenosis that was insignificant at rest may produce a significant pressure drop. This is the basis of post-exercise ankle pressure testing.
exam2.hint: Pressure drop across a stenosis depends on how much flow is being pushed through it.

exam2.question: Using the simplified Bernoulli equation, what is the estimated pressure gradient across a stenosis with a peak jet velocity of 3 m/s, assuming the proximal velocity is negligible?

options.text: 12 mmHg
9 mmHg
36 mmHg
48 mmHg

exam2.explanation: The simplified Bernoulli equation is pressure gradient = 4 times velocity squared, with velocity in m/s and pressure in mmHg: 4 x 3 squared = 4 x 9 = 36 mmHg. An answer of 12 mmHg results from forgetting to square the velocity, and 9 mmHg from forgetting to multiply by 4.
exam2.hint: Square the velocity in meters per second before multiplying by the constant.

exam2.question: What is the fundamental driving force that causes blood to flow from one point to another in the arterial system?

options.text: A difference in total fluid energy between the two points
A difference in vessel diameter between the two points
A difference in blood viscosity between the two points
A difference in hydrostatic pressure alone between the two points

exam2.explanation: Blood flows from a region of higher total energy to one of lower total energy, where total energy includes pressure (potential) energy, kinetic energy and gravitational energy. Hydrostatic pressure is only one component, which is why blood can flow upward from the feet to the heart even though gravitational energy is lower at the feet.
exam2.hint: Consider the combined energy forms, not just one pressure term.

exam2.question: In a normal, straight arterial segment with laminar flow, where should a small pulsed-wave sample volume be placed to record a representative peak systolic velocity?

options.text: Close to the near wall, where the color is brightest
In the center of the lumen, where the flow stream is fastest
Along the far wall, to avoid color artifacts
Straddling the vessel wall, to include the whole lumen

exam2.explanation: In laminar flow the velocity profile is parabolic, with the fastest red cells in the center stream and slower layers near the walls. A small sample volume centered in the lumen, with proper angle correction, records the true peak velocity. Sampling near either wall records the slower layers and underestimates velocity, and including the wall adds clutter and artifactual broadening.
exam2.hint: Recall the shape of the velocity profile in laminar flow.

exam2.question: What is the most likely effect of setting the spectral Doppler gain too high?

options.text: Loss of low-velocity diastolic flow from the display
Aliasing caused by a lower Nyquist limit
Increased acoustic output and higher mechanical index
Spectral blooming with background noise that can cause overestimation of peak velocity

exam2.explanation: Excessive receiver gain amplifies weak signals and noise, making the spectral trace look broader and taller (blooming), filling the background with speckle and potentially leading to overestimation of peak velocity. Gain is a receiver setting, so it does not change the transmitted output or the Nyquist limit; loss of low-velocity flow is typically caused by a high wall filter.
exam2.hint: Gain amplifies everything the receiver hears, including noise.

exam2.question: A sonographer needs to measure acceleration time precisely in a renal hilar artery waveform. Which spectral display adjustment best improves the accuracy of this measurement?

options.text: Increase the sweep speed to spread out each cardiac cycle
Decrease the sweep speed to show more cardiac cycles
Raise the baseline to the top of the display
Increase the wall filter setting

exam2.explanation: A faster sweep speed displays fewer cycles but stretches each one horizontally, so the systolic upstroke is wider and time intervals such as acceleration time can be measured more precisely. A slower sweep compresses the upstroke, making timing measurements less accurate, and the wall filter can actually remove part of the waveform.
exam2.hint: Time measurements are easier when each waveform is spread across more of the screen.

exam2.question: Which statement about moving the spectral Doppler baseline is correct?

options.text: It increases the pulse repetition frequency
It increases the total range of velocities that can be displayed
It redistributes the display between forward and reverse flow without changing the total velocity range
It reduces the Doppler angle used in velocity calculations

exam2.explanation: Shifting the baseline assigns more of the fixed display range to one flow direction and less to the other; the total range, set by the pulse repetition frequency (Nyquist limit), does not change. It can eliminate aliasing when flow is mainly in one direction, but it does not alter PRF or the angle correction.
exam2.hint: Think of the display as a fixed-length ruler whose zero point is being moved.

exam2.question: As part of a laboratory quality assurance program, which device is most appropriate for checking the accuracy of Doppler velocity measurements?

options.text: A tissue-mimicking phantom with nylon line targets
A moving string (or flow) Doppler phantom with a known velocity
A hydrophone used to measure acoustic output
A beam profiler test object for slice thickness

exam2.explanation: A string phantom moves a target at a precisely known speed (and a flow phantom pumps blood-mimicking fluid at a known rate), so measured Doppler velocities can be compared with the true value. A tissue-mimicking phantom with line targets tests gray-scale functions such as depth calibration, resolution and dead zone, not Doppler velocity accuracy.
exam2.hint: Velocity accuracy can only be checked against a target whose speed is already known.

exam2.question: Which bioeffects index is most appropriate to monitor during a transcranial Doppler exam through the temporal bone in an adult?

options.text: Thermal index for soft tissue (TIS)
Thermal index for bone (TIB)
Mechanical index (MI) only
Cranial bone thermal index (TIC)

exam2.explanation: The cranial bone thermal index models heating when bone lies at or near the skin surface, as with a transducer placed on the temporal bone, making it the appropriate thermal index for transcranial studies. The bone thermal index (TIB) models bone located at the focus deeper in the tissue, as in fetal imaging, and the mechanical index addresses nonthermal (cavitation) effects rather than bone heating.
exam2.hint: Choose the index whose model places bone right under the transducer.

exam2.question: A laboratory compares carotid duplex with CT angiography for detecting 70 percent or greater ICA stenosis. CTA finds 50 arteries with 70 percent or greater stenosis; duplex correctly identifies 45 of them. Of the 150 arteries without significant stenosis on CTA, duplex calls 10 positive. What is the sensitivity of duplex?

options.text: 82 percent
93 percent
90 percent
95 percent

exam2.explanation: Sensitivity is true positives divided by all patients with disease: 45 / 50 = 90 percent. The 82 percent value is the positive predictive value, 45 / (45 + 10), and 93 percent is the specificity, 140 / 150.
exam2.hint: Use only the arteries that truly have the disease as your denominator.

exam2.question: In a validation study of renal artery duplex against angiography, the results are: true positives 30, false negatives 10, false positives 6 and true negatives 114. What is the specificity of duplex?

options.text: 95 percent
75 percent
83 percent
92 percent

exam2.explanation: Specificity is true negatives divided by all patients without disease: 114 / (114 + 6) = 114 / 120 = 95 percent. The 75 percent value is the sensitivity, 30 / 40, and 83 percent is the positive predictive value, 30 / 36.
exam2.hint: Start with the patients the gold standard says are normal.

exam2.question: Of 200 lower extremity arterial duplex exams, 50 are called positive for a significant stenosis and 150 are called negative. Angiography confirms disease in 45 of the positive exams and finds significant stenosis in 6 of the negative exams. What is the negative predictive value of duplex?

options.text: 90 percent
88 percent
94.5 percent
96 percent

exam2.explanation: Negative predictive value is true negatives divided by all negative test results: 144 / 150 = 96 percent. The 90 percent value is the positive predictive value (45 / 50), 88 percent is the sensitivity (45 / 51), and 94.5 percent is the overall accuracy (189 / 200).
exam2.hint: Look only at the exams that duplex called negative and ask how many were truly normal.

exam2.question: A carotid duplex validation study yields 40 true positives, 130 true negatives, 20 false positives and 10 false negatives. What is the overall accuracy of the test?

options.text: 80 percent
85 percent
87 percent
67 percent

exam2.explanation: Accuracy is all correct results divided by all exams: (40 + 130) / 200 = 170 / 200 = 85 percent. The 80 percent value is the sensitivity (40 / 50), 87 percent is the specificity (130 / 150), and 67 percent is the positive predictive value (40 / 60).
exam2.hint: Add every result that agreed with the gold standard and divide by the total number of exams.

exam2.question: When duplex velocity criteria are correlated with angiography using the NASCET method, the residual lumen diameter at the stenosis is compared with which reference diameter?

options.text: The diameter of the normal distal internal carotid artery beyond the bulb
The estimated original diameter of the carotid bulb at the stenosis
The diameter of the proximal common carotid artery
The diameter of the contralateral internal carotid artery

exam2.explanation: The NASCET method calculates percent stenosis as one minus the residual lumen divided by the diameter of the normal distal cervical ICA. The ECST method instead uses the estimated original bulb diameter at the site of the stenosis, which gives higher percentages for the same lesion, so labs must know which method their velocity criteria were validated against.
exam2.hint: This method uses a reference segment that can be measured directly on the angiogram downstream of the lesion.

exam2.question: A vascular laboratory is preparing for accreditation by the IAC. Which element is a standard part of the quality improvement requirements?

options.text: Repeating every abnormal exam within 24 hours by a second sonographer
Referring every positive duplex result for confirmatory angiography
Periodic comparison of a sample of exam results with correlative imaging or surgical findings, with review of discrepancies
Replacing ultrasound equipment at fixed intervals regardless of performance

exam2.explanation: Accreditation standards require an ongoing quality improvement program that includes comparing a sample of the lab's results with correlative studies (such as angiography, CTA, MRA or surgical findings) and reviewing discrepancies, along with technical and interpretive quality review. They do not require routine angiography for every positive exam, duplicate scanning of all abnormal studies, or fixed-interval equipment replacement.
exam2.hint: Accreditation focuses on whether the lab checks its own results against an independent reference.

exam2.question: Two years after endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR), color Doppler shows flow inside the aneurysm sac but outside the stent graft, near the posterior sac wall. The flow connects to a lumbar artery and has a to-and-fro spectral pattern. No flow is seen at the proximal or distal attachment sites. Which type of endoleak is most likely?

options.text: Type I
Type II
Type III
Type IV

exam2.explanation: A type II endoleak is retrograde filling of the sac from a branch vessel such as a lumbar artery or the inferior mesenteric artery, often with a to-and-fro waveform. It is the most common endoleak type. A type I endoleak would arise at an attachment site, which was not the case here.
exam2.hint: Ask where the blood entering the sac is coming from: an attachment site, a graft defect, or a native branch vessel.

exam2.question: Which type of endoleak after EVAR is caused by an inadequate seal at the proximal or distal attachment site of the stent graft?

options.text: Type II
Type III
Type IV
Type I

exam2.explanation: A type I endoleak is flow around the graft at the proximal (Ia) or distal (Ib) attachment site. The sac is exposed directly to systemic pressure, so it usually needs prompt treatment. A type III endoleak comes from separated graft components or a fabric tear, not from the seal zone.
exam2.hint: Recall how endoleaks are classified according to the source of flow entering the sac.

exam2.question: On EVAR surveillance, the aneurysm sac has grown from 5.6 cm to 6.3 cm over 1 year. Careful color and power Doppler with low PRF settings shows no flow in the sac, and the graft components are intact. Which term best describes this situation?

options.text: Endotension (type V endoleak)
Type IV endoleak from graft porosity
Normal post-EVAR sac remodeling
Complete sac thrombosis

exam2.explanation: Endotension, sometimes called a type V endoleak, is continued sac enlargement with no endoleak visible on imaging. A successful repair should lead to a stable or shrinking sac, so growth is never normal remodeling. A type IV endoleak from graft porosity is seen around the time of implantation and usually resolves once anticoagulation is reversed.
exam2.hint: A successful repair should leave the sac stable or shrinking, so ask what growth means when no flow is seen.

exam2.question: A 70-year-old man has an asymptomatic popliteal artery aneurysm on duplex. According to current vascular surgery guidelines, at what diameter is elective repair generally recommended?

options.text: 1.0 cm
3.5 cm
2.0 cm
5.5 cm

exam2.explanation: Society for Vascular Surgery guidelines recommend repair of asymptomatic popliteal artery aneurysms 2.0 cm or larger, and smaller aneurysms with significant mural thrombus may also be treated. Popliteal aneurysms rarely rupture; their main risks are thrombosis and distal embolization causing acute limb ischemia, so the threshold is far below the 5.5 cm used for abdominal aortic aneurysms in men.
exam2.hint: The main danger of this aneurysm is thrombosis and embolization rather than rupture.

exam2.question: Renal duplex shows segmental arteries in the right kidney with a slow systolic upstroke, rounded systolic peaks, and an acceleration time of 0.12 s. The left kidney segmental arteries have a sharp upstroke with an acceleration time of 0.04 s. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Right renal vein thrombosis
Significant stenosis of the right main renal artery
Intrinsic parenchymal disease of the right kidney
Obstructive hydronephrosis of the right kidney

exam2.explanation: A tardus-parvus waveform with an acceleration time longer than about 0.07 s in the intrarenal arteries suggests a significant stenosis upstream in the main renal artery. Parenchymal disease and obstruction raise intrarenal resistance (higher RI) but do not delay the systolic upstroke.
exam2.hint: A delayed systolic upstroke downstream points to a problem upstream.

exam2.question: An interlobar renal artery has a peak systolic velocity of 40 cm/s and an end-diastolic velocity of 12 cm/s. What is the resistive index?
exam2.explanation: The resistive index equals (PSV minus EDV) divided by PSV: (40 - 12) / 40 = 0.70. A value of 0.30 is EDV divided by PSV, and 3.33 is PSV divided by EDV, which are common calculation errors.
exam2.hint: Subtract the diastolic velocity from the systolic velocity, then divide by the systolic velocity.

exam2.question: During renal artery duplex, bowel gas blocks the view of the right renal artery from the anterior midline approach. Which approach is most likely to show the right renal artery from its origin?

options.text: Stay anterior and raise the color gain until the artery fills
Turn the patient prone and scan the proximal artery from the back
Sit the patient upright and use a sagittal subxiphoid view
Use a coronal flank view through the kidney with the patient in left lateral decubitus

exam2.explanation: With the patient lying on the left side, a coronal view through the right flank uses the liver and kidney as acoustic windows. This view can show the aorta with both renal arteries arising from it (the 'banana peel' view). A prone approach is useful for the kidney itself but is too far from the aorta to show the renal artery origin well.
exam2.hint: Use solid organs as an acoustic window and move the gas-filled bowel out of the way.

exam2.question: A patient with diabetes and rising creatinine has echogenic kidneys. Both main renal arteries have normal peak systolic velocities and a normal renal-aortic ratio, but the intrarenal resistive index is 0.85 on both sides. What do these findings most likely indicate?

options.text: Bilateral main renal artery stenosis
Bilateral fibromuscular dysplasia
Intrinsic renal parenchymal disease
A normal finding in an adult kidney

exam2.explanation: An intrarenal RI above about 0.70 in an adult suggests increased resistance in the kidney itself, as seen in medical renal disease such as diabetic nephropathy. Main renal artery stenosis would show high velocities at the stenosis and tends to lower the downstream RI with a tardus-parvus pattern.
exam2.hint: Consider where resistance is raised when the main arteries are normal but the intrarenal waveforms are not.

exam2.question: In a patient with a chronically occluded celiac artery, the liver and spleen are perfused through collaterals from the superior mesenteric artery. Which pathway usually carries this collateral flow?

options.text: Pancreaticoduodenal arcades to the gastroduodenal artery
Arc of Riolan between the middle and left colic arteries
Internal mammary to inferior epigastric arteries
Left gastric artery to the esophageal branches

exam2.explanation: The pancreaticoduodenal arcades link the SMA (inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery) to the celiac system (superior pancreaticoduodenal and gastroduodenal arteries). When the celiac artery is occluded, flow in the gastroduodenal artery reverses toward the common hepatic artery. The arc of Riolan connects the SMA and IMA, not the SMA and celiac artery.
exam2.hint: Look for the collateral that runs around the head of the pancreas and duodenum.

exam2.question: A thin 30-year-old woman has postprandial epigastric pain. The celiac artery has no plaque. Its peak systolic velocity is 310 cm/s at end-expiration and falls to 150 cm/s at deep inspiration, and the celiac artery looks hooked upward during expiration. The SMA is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Atherosclerotic celiac artery stenosis
Median arcuate ligament compression
Celiac artery dissection
Superior mesenteric artery syndrome

exam2.explanation: The median arcuate ligament can compress the celiac artery during expiration. Velocities are higher in expiration and normalize or improve in deep inspiration as the artery moves away from the ligament. A fixed atherosclerotic stenosis would not change much with breathing, and superior mesenteric artery syndrome is compression of the duodenum, not the celiac artery.
exam2.hint: Ask why a stenosis would change with breathing.

exam2.question: In Budd-Chiari syndrome, the caudate lobe of the liver is often enlarged while the rest of the liver atrophies. Why?

options.text: It has a dual supply from the hepatic artery and portal vein
It sits closest to the main portal vein bifurcation
Its veins drain directly into the IVC and bypass the blocked hepatic veins
It receives collateral flow from the recanalized umbilical vein

exam2.explanation: Small caudate veins drain straight into the IVC, so the caudate lobe keeps its venous outflow when the main hepatic veins are blocked, and it hypertrophies. The whole liver has a dual hepatic artery and portal vein supply, so that does not explain why only the caudate lobe is spared.
exam2.hint: Budd-Chiari is an outflow problem, so think about how the caudate lobe drains.

exam2.question: In a patient with cirrhosis, which main portal vein finding is most specific for advanced portal hypertension?

options.text: A main portal vein diameter of 11 mm
Hepatopetal flow of 25 cm/s with mild phasicity
Slight respiratory variation in portal vein velocity
Hepatofugal (reversed) flow away from the liver

exam2.explanation: Normal portal flow is hepatopetal (toward the liver), mildly phasic, and usually about 15 to 40 cm/s. Hepatofugal flow means portal pressure exceeds sinusoidal outflow capacity, so blood is being diverted into portosystemic collaterals, which is a specific sign of advanced portal hypertension. A diameter of 11 mm is within normal limits.
exam2.hint: Choose the finding that could never be seen in a normal liver.

exam2.question: A patient with a history of severe pancreatitis has no identifiable main portal vein. Instead, many small, tortuous channels in the porta hepatis carry low-velocity, continuous venous flow toward the liver. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: A recanalized paraumbilical vein
Chronic portal vein thrombosis with cavernous transformation
A hepatic artery aneurysm
Acute Budd-Chiari syndrome

exam2.explanation: Cavernous transformation is a network of periportal collateral veins that forms after chronic portal vein occlusion and carries hepatopetal flow around the blocked segment. Pancreatitis is a known cause of portal and splenic vein thrombosis. A recanalized paraumbilical vein runs in the ligamentum teres and carries flow away from the liver.
exam2.hint: Consider what the body builds around a vein that has been blocked for a long time.

exam2.question: Four months after kidney transplantation, a patient has new hypertension and rising creatinine. Duplex shows a peak systolic velocity of 340 cm/s with post-stenotic turbulence in the transplant renal artery near the anastomosis, and tardus-parvus waveforms in the intrarenal arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Transplant renal artery stenosis
Acute rejection
Transplant renal vein thrombosis
Acute tubular necrosis

exam2.explanation: A focal high velocity (often over 250 cm/s) with turbulence at the anastomosis, together with dampened intrarenal waveforms downstream, indicates transplant renal artery stenosis. It typically appears months after surgery. Rejection and acute tubular necrosis raise intrarenal resistance but do not cause a focal velocity jump or a tardus-parvus pattern.
exam2.hint: A focal velocity jump plus dampened flow downstream is the classic pairing for a narrowing.

exam2.question: Three days after kidney transplantation, the graft is swollen and tender. No flow is detected in the main renal vein, and the intrarenal arteries show sharp systolic peaks with reversed, plateau-like flow throughout diastole. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Transplant renal artery stenosis
Perinephric lymphocele
Arteriovenous fistula after biopsy
Transplant renal vein thrombosis

exam2.explanation: When the renal vein is occluded, outflow is blocked and intrarenal arterial diastolic flow reverses. Absent venous flow and an enlarged graft in the early postoperative period complete the picture of renal vein thrombosis. Renal artery stenosis would cause tardus-parvus waveforms, not reversed diastolic flow.
exam2.hint: Think about what happens to arterial diastolic flow when the outflow from an organ is completely blocked.

exam2.question: After a biopsy of a transplant kidney, color Doppler shows a focal area of aliasing with a speckled color artifact in the surrounding tissue. The feeding artery has high-velocity, low-resistance flow, and the adjacent vein shows pulsatile, arterial-looking flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Pseudoaneurysm
Renal vein thrombosis
Arteriovenous fistula
Subcapsular hematoma

exam2.explanation: An arteriovenous fistula sends arterial blood straight into a vein. This causes high-velocity, low-resistance arterial flow, an arterialized venous waveform, and tissue vibration that appears as a color speckle artifact. A pseudoaneurysm would show a rounded sac with swirling (yin-yang) flow and to-and-fro flow in its neck.
exam2.hint: Look for the clue that arterial blood is entering a vein directly.

exam2.question: A patient with a radiocephalic arteriovenous fistula has a cold, painful hand during dialysis. Flow in the radial artery distal to the anastomosis is reversed, and it becomes antegrade when the fistula outflow vein is manually compressed. What do these findings suggest?

options.text: Access-related hand ischemia from arterial steal
Stenosis of the venous outflow
Central venous stenosis
Early thrombosis of the fistula

exam2.explanation: The low-resistance fistula can pull blood backward from the distal radial artery and the palmar arch, taking it away from the hand. Reversed distal flow that becomes antegrade with fistula compression, together with ischemic symptoms, supports clinically significant steal. Outflow and central venous stenoses cause arm swelling or access dysfunction, not reversal of distal arterial flow.
exam2.hint: Ask where the hand's blood supply is going when compressing the fistula restores normal flow direction.

exam2.question: During pre-operative arterial mapping for a radiocephalic arteriovenous fistula, what minimum radial artery inner diameter at the wrist is most commonly used to predict a successful fistula?

options.text: 1.0 mm
2.0 mm
3.5 mm
5.0 mm

exam2.explanation: Most mapping protocols use an arterial inner diameter of at least 2.0 mm, because smaller arteries are linked to poor fistula maturation. A 1.0 mm artery is too small, and requiring 3.5 mm or more would exclude many arteries that work well.
exam2.hint: The arterial threshold is a little smaller than the commonly used vein threshold.

exam2.question: A 22-year-old competitive swimmer has sudden swelling and a bluish color of the right arm after an intense training session. Duplex shows occlusive thrombus in the right subclavian and axillary veins. There is no central line or other catheter. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Catheter-related venous thrombosis
Superior vena cava syndrome
Superficial thrombophlebitis of the cephalic vein
Effort thrombosis (Paget-Schroetter syndrome)

exam2.explanation: Paget-Schroetter syndrome is primary thrombosis of the subclavian-axillary vein in young, active people. It is caused by repeated compression of the vein at the costoclavicular space (venous thoracic outlet syndrome) during overhead activity. With no catheter present, catheter-related thrombosis is unlikely, and SVC syndrome would cause bilateral arm, head, and neck swelling.
exam2.hint: Think about a young athlete who uses repetitive overhead arm motion and has no catheter.

exam2.question: The mid subclavian vein lies behind the clavicle and cannot be compressed with the transducer. Which technique is most appropriate for evaluating this segment for thrombus?

options.text: Apply firm compression through the clavicle
Rely only on gray-scale to look for echogenic material
Use color and spectral Doppler, including phasicity and the response to a sniff
Record the segment as not evaluated and skip it

exam2.explanation: Where compression is impossible, the exam relies on complete color filling, spectral waveforms with normal respiratory phasicity and cardiac pulsatility, and a brief collapse with a quick sniff. Acute thrombus can be nearly anechoic, so gray-scale imaging alone can miss it.
exam2.hint: If you cannot squeeze the vein, look at how blood flows through it.

exam2.question: The right internal jugular and right subclavian veins are compressible where tested, but their Doppler signals are continuous and nonphasic, with no cardiac pulsatility and no response to a sniff. The left-sided veins show normal pulsatile, phasic flow. Where is an obstruction most likely located?

options.text: Right axillary vein
Right brachiocephalic vein
Superior vena cava
Right basilic vein

exam2.explanation: Normal upper extremity and neck veins transmit cardiac and respiratory pulsations from the chest. Losing these signals in both the IJ and subclavian veins points to an obstruction central to their confluence, in the right brachiocephalic vein. SVC obstruction would usually affect both sides, and an axillary vein obstruction is downstream of the abnormal segments, so it would not explain them.
exam2.hint: Find the closest vein toward the heart that both abnormal veins drain into but the left side does not.

exam2.question: A patient with a large right renal mass has echogenic material extending from the right renal vein into an expanded IVC. Color and spectral Doppler show low-resistance arterial flow inside this material. What does this most likely represent?

options.text: Tumor thrombus
Bland (non-tumor) thrombus
An IVC filter with trapped clot
An inflow mixing artifact from the renal vein

exam2.explanation: Arterial flow inside an intraluminal venous mass shows that it has its own blood supply, which is typical of tumor thrombus, as seen with renal cell carcinoma. Bland thrombus has no internal arterial flow. An inflow mixing artifact would not expand the vein or contain arterial waveforms.
exam2.hint: Bland clot does not have its own blood supply.

exam2.question: In a supine patient, the posterior tibial veins at the ankle are fully compressible, but no spontaneous Doppler flow is detected in them. A brisk venous signal appears when the foot is squeezed. How is this best interpreted?

options.text: Acute occlusive thrombus in the posterior tibial veins
Obstruction of the ipsilateral iliac vein
A normal finding, because small distal veins often lack spontaneous flow at rest
Valvular incompetence of the posterior tibial veins

exam2.explanation: Flow velocities in small calf veins of a resting supine patient are often too low to detect, so absent spontaneous flow is common and not abnormal there. Full compressibility and brisk augmentation with distal compression confirm patency. Occlusive thrombus would make the veins noncompressible and abolish augmentation, central obstruction is assessed by phasicity at the common femoral vein, and incompetence is shown by retrograde flow after compression is released.
exam2.hint: Consider how fast blood moves in small calf veins at rest, and what the response to squeezing the foot shows.

exam2.question: A woman with chronic pelvic pain and vulvar varicosities is evaluated for pelvic congestion syndrome. Which duplex finding best supports this diagnosis?

options.text: Normal-caliber left ovarian vein with cephalad flow toward the renal vein
High-resistance flow in the uterine arteries
Normal respiratory phasicity in both external iliac veins
Dilated left ovarian vein with retrograde (caudal) flow that increases with Valsalva

exam2.explanation: Pelvic congestion syndrome is usually caused by incompetent ovarian veins, most often on the left. A dilated vein carries reversed flow downward into dilated parauterine and pelvic varices, especially with Valsalva or upright positioning. Normal ovarian vein flow is cephalad toward the left renal vein or IVC.
exam2.hint: Think about which direction ovarian vein flow should normally go, and what happens when the valves fail.

exam2.question: A patient has varicose veins on the posterior and lateral calf. The great saphenous vein is competent along its whole length. Reflux in which vein most likely explains this pattern?

options.text: Small saphenous vein
Anterior accessory saphenous vein
Posterior tibial veins
Femoral vein

exam2.explanation: The small saphenous vein runs up the posterior calf from behind the lateral malleolus. Reflux, often starting at the saphenopopliteal junction, typically feeds varicosities on the posterior and lateral calf. The anterior accessory saphenous vein usually causes varicosities on the anterior and lateral thigh.
exam2.hint: Match where the varicosities are with the superficial vein that drains that area.

exam2.question: Which description best fits a typical venous leg ulcer?

options.text: Deep, punched-out ulcer on the toes with a pale base and severe pain at night
Shallow ulcer with irregular borders above the medial malleolus, with surrounding hyperpigmentation
Painless ulcer under the first metatarsal head with surrounding callus
Dry, black area of tissue loss at the tip of the great toe

exam2.explanation: Venous ulcers usually occur in the gaiter area, most often above the medial malleolus. They are shallow with irregular edges and are surrounded by skin changes such as hyperpigmentation and lipodermatosclerosis. Deep, punched-out, painful ulcers on the toes are typical of arterial disease, and plantar ulcers over pressure points are typical of diabetic neuropathy.
exam2.hint: Venous ulcers form where venous pressure and skin changes are worst, in the lower inner leg.

exam2.question: A patient has varicose veins and firm, indurated, tight skin with fibrosis of the lower medial leg (lipodermatosclerosis). There is no ulcer and no history of one. What is the correct CEAP clinical class?

options.text: C3
C4a
C5
C4b

exam2.explanation: In CEAP, C4a covers pigmentation and eczema, while C4b covers lipodermatosclerosis and atrophie blanche, which signal a higher risk of ulceration. C3 is edema alone, and C5 needs a healed ulcer.
exam2.hint: Class 4 skin changes are split into two subgroups by how severe they are.

exam2.question: A patient with a documented femoral-popliteal DVT 5 years ago now has leg swelling and skin changes from chronic venous insufficiency. How is the etiologic (E) component of CEAP classified?

options.text: Ep (primary)
Ec (congenital)
Es (secondary)
En (no venous cause identified)

exam2.explanation: Venous disease that develops after a known event such as DVT is secondary (Es). Post-thrombotic disease is the most common form. Primary (Ep) disease comes from degenerative valve or wall weakness without a known cause.
exam2.hint: The E component asks whether the disease came from an identifiable earlier event.

exam2.question: Which patient position is preferred for a lower extremity venous reflux exam?

options.text: Supine and flat, with the leg straight
Standing, with weight on the opposite leg and the examined leg relaxed
Prone, with the feet hanging over the end of the table
Trendelenburg, with the head lower than the feet

exam2.explanation: Reflux is best shown with gravity applying a full hydrostatic column, ideally with the patient standing. Weight is placed on the opposite leg so the examined leg's muscles are relaxed and its veins fill. Supine and Trendelenburg positions reduce venous filling and can cause valve closure to be missed or reflux to be underestimated.
exam2.hint: Valve failure is most obvious when gravity is pulling blood down the leg.

exam2.question: Thrombus in which upper extremity vein is classified as a deep vein thrombosis?

options.text: Brachial veins
Cephalic vein
Basilic vein
Median cubital vein

exam2.explanation: The paired brachial veins run with the brachial artery and are deep veins, so thrombus in them is a DVT. The cephalic, basilic, and median cubital veins are superficial veins, so thrombus there is superficial venous thrombosis, although basilic thrombus near the axillary vein deserves attention.
exam2.hint: Ask which of these veins lies beneath the deep fascia.

exam2.question: Where does the right gonadal (ovarian or testicular) vein normally drain?

options.text: Right renal vein
Right common iliac vein
Inferior vena cava
Left renal vein

exam2.explanation: The right gonadal vein usually enters the anterior IVC just below the right renal vein. The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, which is why left renal vein compression can lead to left-sided varicoceles and pelvic varices.
exam2.hint: The left and right gonadal veins do not drain the same way.

exam2.question: Which vein is longer and crosses the midline in the upper chest to join its counterpart and form the superior vena cava?

options.text: Right brachiocephalic vein
Azygos vein
Left subclavian vein
Left brachiocephalic vein

exam2.explanation: Because the SVC lies to the right of midline, the left brachiocephalic vein must cross from left to right, passing anterior to the aortic arch branches. It is therefore longer than the short, nearly vertical right brachiocephalic vein. The azygos vein drains into the posterior SVC but does not form it.
exam2.hint: The SVC is on the right side of the chest, so one tributary has farther to travel.

exam2.question: Which veins enter the inferior vena cava at the most superior (cephalad) level?

options.text: Hepatic veins
Renal veins
Right gonadal vein
Lumbar veins

exam2.explanation: The hepatic veins enter the IVC just below the diaphragm, near the right atrium, making them the highest major tributaries. The renal veins enter at about L1 to L2, the right gonadal vein enters below them, and the lumbar veins enter along the lower IVC.
exam2.hint: Picture the course of the IVC from the pelvis up to the right atrium.

exam2.question: In the upper arm, which superficial vein joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein?

options.text: Cephalic vein
Basilic vein
Median cubital vein
Radial vein

exam2.explanation: The basilic vein runs up the medial arm, pierces the deep fascia, and joins the brachial veins near the lower border of the teres major to form the axillary vein. The cephalic vein runs along the lateral arm in the deltopectoral groove and drains into the axillary vein higher up.
exam2.hint: Ask which superficial vein pierces the deep fascia in the mid upper arm.

exam2.question: A patient returns 48 to 72 hours after endovenous thermal ablation of the great saphenous vein. What is the main purpose of this early duplex exam?

options.text: Confirm that the ablated vein has fully disappeared
Measure ankle-brachial indices to check arterial injury
Map perforating veins for a second procedure
Look for thrombus extending from the ablated vein into the common femoral vein

exam2.explanation: The early post-ablation scan checks for endovenous heat-induced thrombosis (EHIT), meaning thrombus extending from the treated vein across the saphenofemoral junction into the common femoral vein, and it also screens for DVT. The ablated vein normally stays visible as a thickened, noncompressible cord for months, so it is not expected to disappear early.
exam2.hint: The main early risk is at the junction of the treated superficial vein with the deep system.

exam2.question: During endovenous thermal ablation, tumescent anesthetic fluid is injected around the vein within its fascial compartment. What does this accomplish?

options.text: It distends the vein so the catheter passes more easily
It provides local anticoagulation to prevent EHIT
It compresses the vein onto the catheter, numbs the area, and absorbs heat to protect surrounding tissue
It increases blood flow through the vein to cool the catheter tip

exam2.explanation: Tumescent fluid compresses and empties the vein so the vein wall contacts the heat source. It also provides anesthesia and acts as a heat sink that separates the vein from skin and nerves. Distending the vein would reduce wall contact and make ablation less effective.
exam2.hint: Ablation works best when the vein wall is pressed against the heat source and nearby tissue is protected.

exam2.question: Before ultrasound-guided percutaneous access of the great saphenous vein for thermal ablation, which patient position helps most?

options.text: Trendelenburg, to empty the vein
Reverse Trendelenburg, to distend the vein
Supine, with the leg raised on pillows
Prone, with the knee flexed

exam2.explanation: Tilting the patient head-up (reverse Trendelenburg) fills the vein with blood, which makes it larger and easier to puncture. After the catheter is placed, the patient is usually tilted head-down (Trendelenburg) for tumescent anesthesia and ablation, so the vein empties.
exam2.hint: A full vein is a bigger target for the needle.

exam2.question: For endovenous thermal ablation of the great saphenous vein, where is the catheter tip usually positioned before treatment begins?

options.text: About 2 cm below (distal to) the saphenofemoral junction
Inside the common femoral vein, 1 cm above the junction
At the level of the knee
Exactly at the saphenofemoral junction ostium

exam2.explanation: The tip is usually placed about 2 cm distal to the saphenofemoral junction, often just below the superficial epigastric vein inflow, and confirmed on ultrasound. This keeps heat away from the deep vein and lowers the risk of EHIT. Placing the tip at or above the junction would expose the common femoral vein to thermal injury and thrombosis.
exam2.hint: Keep the heat source a safe distance from the deep venous system.

exam2.question: How do detergent sclerosants such as polidocanol and sodium tetradecyl sulfate close a treated vein?

options.text: They heat the vein wall until its collagen contracts
They mechanically abrade the vein wall with a rotating wire
They damage the endothelium, causing the vein to thrombose and then fibrose
They dissolve existing thrombus to restore normal flow

exam2.explanation: Detergent sclerosants break down the cell membranes of the endothelium. The injured vein then thromboses, which leads to fibrosis and permanent closure of the vein. Heat-induced collagen contraction is how thermal ablation works, not sclerotherapy.
exam2.hint: Sclerotherapy is a chemical injury to the inner lining of the vein.

exam2.question: Where is an inferior vena cava filter usually placed, and which structures should be identified to guide placement?

options.text: In the suprahepatic IVC, above the hepatic veins
In the common iliac vein on the side of the DVT
In the IVC just above the renal veins, below the hepatic veins
In the infrarenal IVC, with the top of the filter at or just below the lowest renal vein

exam2.explanation: The standard position is infrarenal, with the top of the filter at or just below the lowest renal vein. This catches emboli from the legs and pelvis while keeping any filter thrombus away from the renal veins. Suprarenal placement is used only in special cases, such as thrombus extending into the renal veins or pregnancy.
exam2.hint: If the filter traps clot, which veins do you want to keep clear?

exam2.question: A patient had a left common iliac vein stent placed for iliac vein compression. Earlier follow-up scans showed normal respiratory phasicity in the left common femoral vein. On today's scan, flow there is continuous and nonphasic. What does this change most likely suggest?

options.text: An expected finding in a patent iliac stent
Stenosis or thrombosis of the stent or the veins central to it
Reflux in the left great saphenous vein
Improved outflow after the stent has healed in

exam2.explanation: A new loss of respiratory phasicity in the CFV below an iliac stent suggests that outflow is blocked again, from in-stent stenosis, stent thrombosis, or disease beyond the stent. The stent should be scanned directly for color filling and velocity changes. A patent stent keeps the normal phasic signal in the CFV, so continuous flow is not expected.
exam2.hint: Compare today's waveform with the earlier one and ask what the change means about outflow.

exam2.question: During ultrasound-guided internal jugular vein cannulation using a short-axis (out-of-plane) view, the needle appears as a bright echogenic dot. What is the main limitation of this view?

options.text: The dot may be the needle shaft rather than the tip, so the tip may be deeper than it appears
The vein cannot be told apart from the carotid artery in short axis
The needle cannot be seen at all unless it is perpendicular to the beam
Short-axis imaging requires color Doppler to see the vein

exam2.explanation: In an out-of-plane view, the beam crosses the needle at only one point, so the bright dot may be the shaft while the tip is deeper. This can lead to puncture of the back wall of the vein or the carotid artery. The tip is followed by sliding or fanning the transducer ahead of the needle. Short axis actually shows the vein and carotid artery side by side very well.
exam2.hint: Think about which part of the needle a thin cross-sectional slice actually shows.

exam3.question: A carotid duplex exam shows visible plaque in the proximal left internal carotid artery with a peak systolic velocity of 265 cm/s, an end-diastolic velocity of 110 cm/s, and an ICA/CCA peak systolic velocity ratio of 4.6. Using SRU consensus criteria, how should this stenosis be graded?

options.text: Less than 50%
70% or greater, short of near occlusion
Total occlusion

exam3.explanation: An ICA PSV above 230 cm/s with visible plaque, supported by an ICA/CCA ratio above 4.0 and an EDV above 100 cm/s, falls in the 70% or greater category. The 50% to 69% category requires a PSV of 125 to 230 cm/s, which this velocity clearly exceeds.
exam3.hint: Compare the peak systolic velocity to the upper threshold of the SRU criteria.

exam3.question: A 68-year-old man has heterogeneous plaque in the right internal carotid artery bulb. The ICA peak systolic velocity is 158 cm/s, the end-diastolic velocity is 48 cm/s, and the ICA/CCA ratio is 2.6. Which SRU category best fits these findings?

options.text: Normal, no stenosis
Less than 50% stenosis
70% or greater stenosis
50% to 69% stenosis

exam3.explanation: A PSV between 125 and 230 cm/s with visible plaque, supported by an ICA/CCA ratio of 2 to 4 and an EDV of 40 to 100 cm/s, indicates a 50% to 69% stenosis. A PSV of 158 cm/s is well above the 125 cm/s threshold, so the less than 50% category does not apply.
exam3.hint: Locate 158 cm/s between the two SRU peak systolic velocity thresholds.

exam3.question: Which sonographic finding most reliably distinguishes the external carotid artery from the internal carotid artery?

options.text: Branch vessels arising from it in the neck
A larger diameter than the internal carotid artery
A low-resistance waveform with high diastolic flow
A posterolateral course relative to the internal carotid

exam3.explanation: The internal carotid artery normally has no branches in the neck, so demonstrating branches is the most definitive way to identify the ECA. The ECA has a high-resistance waveform, not a low-resistance one, and it typically lies anteromedial and is usually smaller than the ICA.
exam3.hint: Think about which of the two vessels gives off no extracranial branches.

exam3.question: During a carotid duplex exam, the left vertebral artery waveform shows a sharp mid-systolic deceleration that dips toward, but not below, the baseline, followed by antegrade flow in diastole. The right vertebral artery is normal. What does this most likely indicate?

options.text: Complete subclavian steal from a left subclavian occlusion
Distal left vertebral artery occlusion near the basilar artery
Early (incomplete) subclavian steal from a proximal left subclavian stenosis
A normal variant of vertebral artery flow

exam3.explanation: A mid-systolic notch or deceleration with persistent antegrade flow is the earliest (latent or partial) stage of subclavian steal and indicates a hemodynamically significant proximal subclavian or innominate lesion. Complete steal produces fully reversed vertebral flow throughout the cardiac cycle, which is not described here.
exam3.hint: Consider how vertebral flow changes progressively as a proximal subclavian lesion worsens.

exam3.question: A vertebral artery shows a mid-systolic notch suggestive of a partial subclavian steal. Which maneuver is most useful to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Have the patient perform a Valsalva maneuver while monitoring the vertebral artery
Rotate the patient's head toward the side being examined
Inflate an arm cuff above systolic pressure for several minutes, then release it while monitoring the vertebral artery
Compress the ipsilateral common carotid artery for several seconds

exam3.explanation: Releasing an occluding arm cuff creates reactive hyperemia, lowering arm resistance and increasing demand, which accentuates or completes vertebral flow reversal if a steal is present. Carotid compression is not recommended and does not test the subclavian-to-vertebral pathway.
exam3.hint: The goal is to increase blood demand in the arm on the affected side.

exam3.question: Why do many laboratories use higher velocity thresholds to grade in-stent restenosis after carotid artery stenting than for a native internal carotid artery?

options.text: The stent reduces arterial wall compliance, which raises velocities even without significant narrowing
The stent struts cause aliasing that artificially lowers measured velocities
Stented arteries always develop compensatory dilation that lowers velocities
Doppler angle correction cannot be used inside a stent

exam3.explanation: A stented segment is stiffer than a native artery, so velocities tend to be higher for a given lumen size, and applying native criteria would overestimate restenosis. Stent struts do not lower velocities through aliasing, and angle correction is used in stents just as in native vessels.
exam3.hint: Consider how a metal scaffold changes the mechanical properties of the arterial wall.

exam3.question: During a transcranial Doppler exam through the transtemporal window, a signal at a depth of 45 mm is directed toward the transducer. Which artery is most likely being insonated?

options.text: Anterior cerebral artery
Basilar artery
Ophthalmic artery
Middle cerebral artery

exam3.explanation: The middle cerebral artery is found at roughly 30 to 60 mm through the transtemporal window with flow toward the transducer. The anterior cerebral artery lies deeper (about 60 to 75 mm) and flows away from the transducer, and the basilar artery is examined through the suboccipital window.
exam3.hint: Combine the window, the depth, and the flow direction.

exam3.question: A transcranial Doppler exam in a patient with a head injury shows markedly elevated pulsatility indices with very low diastolic velocities in all intracranial arteries on both sides. Which condition does this pattern most suggest?

options.text: Vasospasm of the middle cerebral arteries
Increased intracranial pressure
An intracranial arteriovenous malformation
Severe stenosis of one proximal internal carotid artery

exam3.explanation: Raised intracranial pressure increases resistance to cerebral perfusion globally, producing high pulsatility and low diastolic flow in every vessel. Vasospasm causes focal velocity elevation, while an AVM and a proximal ICA stenosis tend to lower pulsatility in the affected territory.
exam3.hint: A global, bilateral change points to a cause that affects the entire intracranial space.

exam3.question: A carotid plaque appears predominantly hypoechoic (echolucent) on gray-scale imaging. Which composition does this appearance most likely represent?

options.text: Dense calcification
Mature fibrous tissue
Organized collagen with calcium
Lipid-rich material or intraplaque hemorrhage

exam3.explanation: Echolucent plaque is associated with soft components such as lipid and intraplaque hemorrhage and is considered less stable with higher embolic potential. Calcification is highly echogenic and casts an acoustic shadow, and fibrous tissue is moderately to highly echogenic.
exam3.hint: Softer plaque components reflect less ultrasound.

exam3.question: A 42-year-old woman develops neck pain and a headache after chiropractic neck manipulation. Duplex shows no plaque, but the internal carotid artery lumen tapers smoothly beginning about 2 cm above the bulb, with a high-resistance waveform and little diastolic flow proximally. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Atherosclerotic occlusion at the carotid bifurcation
Internal carotid artery dissection
Carotid body tumor
Normal carotid sinus flow

exam3.explanation: A smooth, tapering lumen distal to the bulb without plaque in a younger patient with neck pain after trauma or manipulation is a classic presentation of spontaneous or traumatic ICA dissection. Atherosclerotic disease typically involves the bulb with visible plaque, which is absent here.
exam3.hint: Note the patient's age, the absence of plaque, and the precipitating event.

exam3.question: Which duplex finding is characteristic of fibromuscular dysplasia of the internal carotid artery?

options.text: Alternating areas of narrowing and dilation with velocity increases and turbulence in the mid-to-distal segment
Heavily calcified plaque with acoustic shadowing at the carotid bulb
A single smooth, long-segment narrowing of the common carotid artery
A hypoechoic mass splaying the internal and external carotid arteries

exam3.explanation: Fibromuscular dysplasia produces a string-of-beads pattern of webs and dilations, seen on duplex as segmental velocity elevation and turbulence, usually away from the bifurcation. Calcified bulb plaque is typical of atherosclerosis, and a mass splaying the bifurcation describes a carotid body tumor.
exam3.hint: Picture the classic angiographic appearance of this nonatherosclerotic disease.

exam3.question: A duplex exam 14 months after carotid endarterectomy shows a smooth, homogeneous narrowing at the endarterectomy site with elevated velocities. Which process is the most likely cause of restenosis at this time?

options.text: Recurrent atherosclerotic plaque
A retained intimal flap from surgery
Myointimal (neointimal) hyperplasia
Arterial wall calcification

exam3.explanation: Restenosis within about the first two years after endarterectomy is usually caused by myointimal hyperplasia, which appears smooth and homogeneous. Recurrent atherosclerosis is the typical cause of restenosis that develops later, usually after two years.
exam3.hint: Restenosis cause depends on how long it has been since surgery.

exam3.question: A patient has a known occlusion of the right internal carotid artery. The left internal carotid artery shows a peak systolic velocity of 145 cm/s with only minimal plaque, and the left CCA velocity is also elevated. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: The left ICA must have a 70% or greater stenosis based on velocity alone
Left vertebral artery steal is lowering the left ICA velocity
Doppler angle error is the only possible explanation
Compensatory increased flow in the left carotid system may overestimate the degree of stenosis

exam3.explanation: When one ICA is occluded, the contralateral carotid often carries increased collateral flow, which raises velocities and can lead to overestimation of stenosis. Using the ICA/CCA ratio and the gray-scale plaque burden helps avoid overgrading in this situation.
exam3.hint: Consider where blood to the right hemisphere must come from.

exam3.question: A vertebral artery measures 1.8 mm in diameter and shows a high-resistance waveform with low diastolic flow, while the contralateral vertebral artery is large with normal low-resistance flow. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: A hypoplastic vertebral artery
Complete subclavian steal
Vertebral artery dissection with pseudoaneurysm
Severe stenosis of the contralateral vertebral artery origin

exam3.explanation: A small vertebral artery (generally under about 2 to 2.5 mm) with high-resistance flow and a large contralateral vessel is typical of vertebral hypoplasia. Subclavian steal produces reversed or notched flow rather than simply a small, high-resistance vessel.
exam3.hint: Compare the size and resistance of the two vertebral arteries.

exam3.question: Which artery is normally the first branch of the external carotid artery?

options.text: Facial artery
Superior thyroid artery
Superficial temporal artery
Ophthalmic artery

exam3.explanation: The superior thyroid artery usually arises from the anterior aspect of the proximal external carotid artery and is its first branch. The ophthalmic artery is the first major branch of the internal carotid artery, not the external carotid, and the superficial temporal is a terminal branch.
exam3.hint: Think about which branch arises most proximally from the anterior surface of the ECA, just above the bifurcation.

exam3.question: The tibioperoneal trunk normally divides into which two arteries?

options.text: Anterior tibial and peroneal arteries
Anterior tibial and posterior tibial arteries
Posterior tibial and peroneal arteries
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries

exam3.explanation: The popliteal artery gives off the anterior tibial artery first, then continues as the tibioperoneal trunk, which divides into the posterior tibial and peroneal arteries. The anterior tibial artery is not a branch of the trunk.
exam3.hint: Remember which tibial artery leaves the popliteal artery before the trunk forms.

exam3.question: At which anatomic landmark does the superficial femoral artery become the popliteal artery?

options.text: The inguinal ligament
The adductor hiatus
The origin of the profunda femoris artery
The knee joint line

exam3.explanation: The superficial femoral artery passes through the adductor (Hunter's) canal and becomes the popliteal artery as it exits through the adductor hiatus. The inguinal ligament marks the transition from the external iliac to the common femoral artery.
exam3.hint: Think about where the artery passes from the front of the thigh to the back of the knee.

exam3.question: The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of which artery?

options.text: Posterior tibial artery
Peroneal artery
Lateral plantar artery
Anterior tibial artery
